Here are the key findings from research studies comparing search engine results overlap between Google and Bing:

## Result Overlap

The overlap between Google and Bing is always under 32%, indicating significant differences in the results returned by these two major search engines. Historical research comparing Google, Bing, and Yahoo showed overlap ranging between 22% and 40%.

## Coverage Differences

Google displays more unique domains in the top results than its competitors. Google provided the highest coverage of the five search engines, and US-based search engines Google and Live Search indexed US sites more effectively than Finnish and French sites.

## Search Result Characteristics

A comprehensive study compared the top 10 results from Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, and Metager, using 3,537 queries generated from Google Trends from Germany and the US. Wikipedia and news websites are the most popular sources overall, and the distribution of domains is consistent across all search engines despite some top sources dominating results.

## Ranking Differences

Recent studies report increased overlap in search results, while ranking algorithms appear to be the leading cause for differences in the presentation of results. Research investigating ranking similarity between Bing and Google showed the search engines differed considerably, with Bing tending to interpret queries more diversely than Google.

Based on the search results, here's what research shows about using Google Scholar alone for systematic reviews:

## Key Findings

Google Scholar's constantly-changing content, algorithms and database structure make it a poor choice for systematic reviews. Many studies have demonstrated that a single search engine does not capture all of the available articles, and using two or more databases provides greater coverage of all possible citations.

## Coverage Issues

Google Scholar alone is not sufficient as the concordance between PubMed and Google Scholar is 30.3% with 20.3% of the articles unique to PubMed. However, the combined coverage of Google Scholar and PubMed is between 85% to 98% of the universe of bioscience articles, which may be sufficient.

## Optimal Database Combinations

Research recommends multiple database combinations. The combination of Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar performed best, achieving an overall recall of 98.3 and 100% recall in 72% of systematic reviews, and optimal searches in systematic reviews should search at least Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar as a minimum requirement.

## Current Practice

The common practice of searching through a limited number of literature databases is inadequate and inappropriate for systematic reviews targeting high quality.

Based on the search results, here's what the Tow Center study found regarding AI search engines and citation problems:

## Key Findings

A Tow Center for Digital Journalism study highlights how AI-driven search tools often fail to credit, or to accurately credit, sources. Collectively, they provided incorrect answers to more than 60 percent of queries.

## Study Details

The Tow Center analysis studies eight AI-powered search tools: Perplexity, Google's AI Overviews, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Meta AI, and Grok. In a study of eight such AI-powered tools, the team ran 1,600 queries in which they fed the bots direct excerpts from actual news articles and asked the programs to identify the source article's headline, original publisher, publish date and URL.

## Main Problems Identified

AI search engines cite syndicated or republished versions rather than providing a citation for the original publisher, which diminishes the visibility of primary news organizations and deprives them of direct traffic. Additionally, some platforms, such as Grok and Gemini, regularly generate broken or fabricated URLs, misleading users and reducing referral traffic to legitimate news sites.

## Performance Variation

Error rates varied significantly, with Perplexity at 37%, ChatGPT Search at 67%, and Grok 3 alarming at 94%.

Based on the search results, here's what research shows about search engine results personalization, localization, and reproducibility:

## Key Findings on Non-Reproducible Results

Studies have found that 11.7% of results show differences due to personalization, but this varies widely by search query and result ranking position. The reproducibility of search results varies significantly depending on query type.

## Variation by Query Category

Different types of queries show different levels of personalization: 82% of results for "what is" queries are identical, while only 43% of results for "gadgets" are identical. Politics is the most personalized query category, followed by places and gadgets.

## Factors Driving Result Variation

When comparing logged-in users against a control group, the two factors with measurable impact were being logged in with a Google account and the IP address of the searching users. Localization of results is one factor driving personalization, with company queries showing store locations relevant to the location of the user.

## Recent Research Findings

More recent studies have found greater variations. One recent audit revealed significant customization based on location and browsing preferences, unlike previous studies that found only mild personalization for general topics.

The research indicates that search results are not fully reproducible when the same query is performed by different users in different locations or with different browsing histories.

Based on the web search results, here's what I found regarding Microsoft's retirement of the Bing Search API and its impact on independent search engines:

## Retirement Timeline and Details

Bing Search APIs will be retired on August 11, 2025. Any existing instances of Bing Search APIs will be decommissioned completely, and the product will no longer be available to be used or new customer signup.

## Impact on Independent Search Engines and Developers

The retirement has significant implications for the search ecosystem:

**Barrier to Competition**: Smaller search engines and independent developers face increased barriers to competing with tech giants, as building and maintaining a comprehensive search index is resource-intensive. The Bing Search APIs have been a crucial resource for startups, independent developers, and alternative search engines like DuckDuckGo, Brave, and You.com. These APIs allowed developers to integrate web, image, video, and news search capabilities into their own applications without the need to build and maintain their own massive web indexes.

**Limited Alternatives**: With Google's search APIs now almost completely shuttered for public use and Bing withdrawing its offering, companies have limited choices: Brave Search API – Offers a privacy-focused, independent index, but scale and coverage may lag behind Bing or Google for niche queries. Mojeek Web Search API – Also an independent crawler, lauded for its privacy stance, but similarly limited in scope and often lacking comprehensive coverage.

**Context**: Microsoft's decision comes after a period of steep price hikes for the Bing APIs-reportedly up to tenfold after the launch of ChatGPT-which had already driven some users to develop their own indexing technologies.

I found no evidence supporting a universal winner — this is a case where the premise, not the ranking, is the problem.

Below I separate what's actually supported from what I'm inferring.

---

## Supported by evidence

**1. Major engines return substantially different results, so no one index subsumes the others.**
A study of the top 10 results from Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, and MetaGer across 3,537 Google Trends queries from Germany and the US found the overlap between Google and Bing is *always under 32%*, and concluded that using alternative engines alongside Google "provides a wider variety in sources" ([arXiv:2207.07330](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07330)). Older work comparing Google, Bing, and Yahoo found overlap in the 22–40% range ([Overlap in the Web Search Results of Google and Bing](https://www.nowpublishers.com/article/OpenAccessDownload/JWS-0005)), and ranking-similarity work found Google and Bing "differed considerably" in how they interpret queries ([ACM CIKM](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2063576.2063858)).

**2. For systematic literature research, single-source searching is documented as inadequate.**
Concordance between PubMed and Google Scholar has been measured at ~30%, with ~20% of articles unique to PubMed ([PMC3544576](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3544576/)). A prospective study of optimal database combinations found that Embase + MEDLINE + Web of Science Core Collection + Google Scholar achieved 98.3% overall recall, and recommended these four as a *minimum* ([Systematic Reviews, 2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-017-0644-y)). This is direct evidence that the best tool is task-dependent and often plural.

**3. Regional leadership is split, and at least partly on relevance grounds.**
Baidu leads mainland China (~60%), Yandex leads Russia (~71%), and Korean search is contested between Naver and Google ([geotargetly](https://geotargetly.com/blog/most-popular-search-engines-by-country), [SearchEngines.Net](https://www.searchengines.net/guides/search-engine-market-share-by-country/)). Google withdrew from China entirely. Note these numbers come from SEO-industry sources of mixed rigor — treat the precise figures as approximate.

**4. AI-answer search has a measured accuracy problem.**
The Tow Center tested eight AI search tools (Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Meta AI, Grok) with 1,600 queries and found collectively >60% incorrect answers on source-identification tasks, with error rates ranging from ~37% (Perplexity) to ~94% (Grok 3), plus fabricated URLs on some platforms ([CJR](https://www.cjr.org/tow_center/we-compared-eight-ai-search-engines-theyre-all-bad-at-citing-news.php), [Nieman Lab](https://www.niemanlab.org/2025/03/ai-search-engines-fail-to-produce-accurate-citations-in-over-60-of-tests-according-to-new-tow-center-study/)). So "AI search" is not a blanket upgrade for citation-critical work.

**5. Results aren't fully reproducible across users.**
Personalization and geolocation measurably change results; one audit found ~11.7% of results differ due to personalization, varying sharply by query type — 82% identical for "what is" queries versus 43% for "gadgets," with politics the most personalized category ([arXiv:2211.11518](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.11518), [Northeastern geolocation study](https://www.khoury.northeastern.edu/home/amislove/publications/Geolocation-IMC.pdf)). "Best" is therefore not even a stable property for a single engine.

**6. The independent-index base is narrowing.**
Microsoft retired the Bing Search APIs on August 11, 2025 ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/lifecycle/announcements/bing-search-api-retirement)), which trade press describes as raising barriers for smaller engines and developers that relied on it ([Computing](https://www.computing.co.uk/news/2025/microsoft-s-plan-to-retire-bing-api-access-and-what-it-means-for-web-search), [ppc.land](https://ppc.land/microsoft-ends-bing-search-apis-on-august-11-alternative-costs-40-483-more/)).

---

## Inference (mine, not directly from a source)

- Because "diversity of sources" is itself a research value (point 1) and different engines lead in different regions (point 3), a *portfolio* strategy dominates any single-engine strategy for serious research. This follows from the evidence but isn't a finding any single study states.
- The overlap findings (1) and the MetaGer↔Bing overlap of up to 78% reported in the same paper suggest many "alternative" engines are partly syndicating a major index, so switching engines buys less independence than it appears to. This is my reading, and it's supported for MetaGer specifically, not for every alternative engine.

- **Market-share figures disagree by source.** Global Google share is reported at ~89.8% by several 2026 SEO trackers, but US and per-country numbers vary meaningfully between them, and South Korea is a clear case: StatCounter puts Google first at ~49.5% while Korean domestic measurement puts Naver first at ~63.8% ([serpsculpt](https://serpsculpt.com/search-engine-statistics-by-country/), [searchengines.net](https://www.searchengines.net/guides/search-engine-market-share-by-country/)). - **Overlap studies disagree on trend direction.** Some recent work reports *increased* overlap between engines relative to older studies ([arXiv:2011.00650](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.00650)), which would weaken (but not eliminate) the diversity argument.

## Where the evidence is genuinely poor

- I found **no rigorous, current, independent head-to-head benchmark of general web search engines on research-quality relevance** across task types. Most comparisons measure *overlap* (how different results are), not *quality* (which results are better). Overlap is not a quality metric.
- Vendor and SEO-blog claims about which engine is "best" are marketing, not measurement, and I'd discount them.
- Market share is a popularity measure and says nothing about research quality — Google's ~90% share is not evidence that it is best for any specific research task.

---

## What I'd actually recommend instead of a winner

Route by task, not by loyalty:

| Task | Reasonable primary | Why |

| General web / broad recall | Google, cross-checked with one non-Google engine | <32% overlap means one engine misses a lot ([arXiv:2207.07330](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07330)) |

| Academic / systematic review | Embase + MEDLINE + Web of Science + Google Scholar | Empirically 98.3% recall; Scholar alone is documented as insufficient ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-017-0644-y)) |
| Non-English / regional | The local leader (Baidu, Yandex, Naver) plus Google | Regional engines lead their markets ([geotargetly](https://geotargetly.com/blog/most-popular-search-engines-by-country)) |
| Citation-critical fact-finding | Any engine, but verify against the primary source | AI answer layers misattribute >60% of the time ([CJR](https://www.cjr.org/tow_center/we-compared-eight-ai-search-engines-theyre-all-bad-at-citing-news.php)) |

One caveat on my own process: this answer is built from web search and page fetches, so it inherits exactly the single-engine bias it describes. Treat the market-share numbers as the weakest links in the chain; the overlap, systematic-review, and Tow Center findings are the load-bearing evidence.
